readingInstruction: Read Acts 27:1-28:31. Paul sails for Rome, endures a storm and a shipwreck, survives a snakebite on Malta, and arrives in the capital. The book ends with Paul under house arrest, preaching the kingdom of God. Notice how Acts ends: without a conclusion, because the story continues.
settingTheScene: Paul is sent to Rome as a prisoner under the centurion Julius, along with Luke and Aristarchus. It is late in the sailing season and dangerous. Luke’s account of the voyage is among the most detailed ancient descriptions of a sea journey. Beyond its drama, the voyage shows God’s faithfulness in carrying out the promise made in 23:11: Paul will testify in Rome.
observation: “When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned” (27:20).
“Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar” (27:24).
“So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told” (27:25).
“And so it was that all were brought safely to land” (27:44).
“And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage” (28:15).
“From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets” (28:23).
“Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen” (28:28).
“Proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance” (28:31).
interpretation:
The voyage begins in good weather but deteriorates. Paul warns that the journey will be dangerous, but the centurion trusts the pilot and the owner of the ship. A violent northeaster, the “Euraquilo,” seizes the ship. For days they are driven, throwing cargo and tackle overboard. “All hope of our being saved was at last abandoned.” Then Paul stands up: an angel of God had stood by him that night and said, “Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.” “So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told.” The prisoner becomes the leader of the ship. When sailors try to escape in the lifeboat, Paul warns the centurion. On the fourteenth night, Paul urges them all to eat, takes bread, gives thanks to God in the presence of all, and breaks it. Two hundred seventy-six people are on board. The ship runs aground, and the soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wishing to save Paul, stops them. All reach land safely, some swimming and some on pieces of the ship.

On Malta, the islanders show unusual kindness. A viper fastens on Paul’s hand, and the people expect him to die; when he shakes it off and suffers no harm, they say he is a god. This is a reversal of Lystra, where they first worshiped and then stoned him. Paul heals the father of the chief man of the island, and the rest of the sick come and are cured. After three months, they sail again for Rome.

Believers meet Paul at the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns, “and on seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage.” In Rome, he is allowed to live by himself with a soldier guarding him. Three days later, he calls the local Jewish leaders and explains why he is in chains: “it is because of the hope of Israel.” They arrange a day, and many come to his lodging. “From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets.” Some are convinced, others disbelieve. Paul quotes Isaiah 6 about hardened hearts and says, “This salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.”

The book ends abruptly: “He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” Luke does not tell us what happened to Paul at the trial. The ending is deliberate: the word of God is not bound (2 Timothy 2:9). The story of the church continues in every generation, including yours. From Jerusalem to Rome, from the upper room to the center of the empire, the gospel has gone out.
connection: Acts 1:8 is the program that is fulfilled here. Psalm 107:23-30 describes sailors rescued from a storm. Jonah 1 is another storm at sea. Isaiah 6:9-10 is the quotation about hardened hearts. Romans 1:8-15 and 15:22-29 reveal Paul’s longing to see Rome. Philippians 1:12-14, Ephesians 6:19-20, Colossians 4:3, and Philemon are letters from this imprisonment. 2 Timothy 4:6-8 is his final testimony. Ephesians 2:19-22 describes the household of God.
application:
Review your own storms. Was God keeping a promise that you couldn’t see?

Read Acts 1:8 again and see how the book has fulfilled it. Where are you in the story?

Take the closing words as a charge: proclaim the kingdom and teach about Jesus with all boldness.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the book of Acts and the word spreading to the ends of the earth.
Thank him for his faithfulness through storms.
Ask him to keep you bold and unhindered.
